marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q001.takeaway: Basal cardiac output in a resting adult is about 5.5 L/min.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q001.displayText:
Basal cardiac output in a resting adult is about 5.5 L/min.

The basal cardiac output in adults is around 5.5 litres.
Cardiac output is given by, Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.

In a resting, supine man cardiac output averages about 5.0 L/min (70 mL x 72 beats/min).
emphasis: Basal cardiac output in a resting adult is about 5

rationales.a: 10 L/min is above resting output and may occur with exercise.
rationales.c: 7.5 L/min exceeds the usual basal adult value.
rationales.d: 6.5 L/min is above the approximate resting reference.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q002.displayText:
Cardiac output is measured by Fick principle, thermodilution or imaging; V/Q ratio assesses pulmonary ventilation-perfusion matching.

VIQ ratio not used to determine cardiac output. »

+ Fick principle

+ Dye dilution/thermodilution

+ Doppler plus echocardiograph

emphasis: Cardiac output is measured by Fick principle, thermodilution or imaging; V/Q ratio assesses pulmonary ventilation-perfusion matching

rationales.a: Fick’s principle estimates output from oxygen consumption and arteriovenous O₂ difference.
rationales.b: Thermodilution is an invasive method to estimate cardiac output.
rationales.c: Echocardiography estimates output from stroke volume and heart rate.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q004.takeaway: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q004.displayText:
Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume.

Ejection fraction is SV/EDV.

The amount of blood ejected by each ventricle per stroke at rest is 70-90 mL. The end-
ventricular volume is about 130 mL. The ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic
ventricular volume that is ejected with each stroke, is about 65%.
emphasis: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume

rationales.a: SV/ESV uses the wrong denominator; EF uses the filled volume before systole.
rationales.b: ESV/EDV is the fraction remaining after contraction, not ejected.
rationales.c: EDV/SV reverses the ejection fraction ratio.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q006.displayText:
End-diastolic volume reflects ventricular filling and is the principal volume determinant of preload.

Volume determining preload is End diastolic volume.

Preload is the initial stretch on muscle at the end of diastole. Preload is equal to End diastolic
volume (EDV) and is determined by venous return to heart.

e
emphasis: End-diastolic volume reflects ventricular filling and is the principal volume determinant of preload

rationales.a: End-systolic volume is what remains after contraction, not the precontraction filling volume.
rationales.b: Aortic blood volume is not the ventricular preload measure.
rationales.c: Ejection volume is the result of contraction, not the filling stretch that defines preload.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q008.takeaway: Gravity raises dependent arterial pressure but does not aid venous return; valves, muscle pump and fascia support return while standing.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q008.displayText:
Gravity raises dependent arterial pressure but does not aid venous return; valves, muscle pump and fascia support return while standing.

Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is not facilitated by increased arterial pressure.
Factors that facilitate venous return to the heart:
+ Calf muscles contract and pump blood through veins.
+ Valves don't allow the retrograde flow of blood through veins.

+ Deep fascia by forming a supporting structure to veins.

507 

Note: The pulsations of artery helps in increasing lymph flow .
emphasis: Gravity raises dependent arterial pressure but does not aid venous return; valves, muscle pump and fascia support return while standing

rationales.a: Calf-muscle contraction compresses deep veins and propels blood upward.
rationales.b: Perforator valves direct flow from superficial to deep veins.
rationales.c: Deep fascia provides resistance against venous expansion and supports the muscle pump.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q009.takeaway: Moving from standing to supine promptly shifts blood centrally and increases venous return.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q009.displayText: Moving from standing to supine promptly shifts blood centrally and increases venous return.
emphasis: Moving from standing to supine promptly shifts blood centrally and increases venous return

rationales.a: Heart rate tends to fall after central blood volume rises and baroreflexes respond.
rationales.c: Cerebral blood flow is autoregulated; the immediate change is central venous return.
rationales.d: Supine posture reduces the apex-base hydrostatic gradient rather than selectively reducing apical flow.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q011.takeaway: The source key applies a simplified parallel-circuit model: removing renal vascular bed is said to raise peripheral resistance/afterload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q011.displayText:
The source key applies a simplified parallel-circuit model: removing renal vascular bed is said to raise peripheral resistance/afterload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output.

Surgical removal of kidney leads to decrease in cardiac output.

Amputation of a limb or surgical removal of organs like kidney removes a parallel circuit
thus increasing total peripheral vascular resistance. As the resistance increases, afterload
increases hence decreasing stroke volume.

CO= HR x SV, therefore decrease in stroke volume leads to decrease in cardiac output.
emphasis: The source key applies a simplified parallel-circuit model: removing renal vascular bed is said to raise peripheral resistance/afterload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output

rationales.b: Increased output contradicts the source model’s increased-afterload and reduced-stroke-volume sequence.
rationales.c: The source explicitly predicts a decrease from the lost parallel circuit; this theoretical key should not be generalized beyond the stated model.
rationales.d: The keyed source explanation gives a specific decrease rather than an unpredictable response.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.
audit.medicalReviewNote: The source derives the keyed decrease from a simplified vascular-resistance model. Preserve the source key while presenting the mechanism as the textbook’s model, not a universal clinical prediction after donation.

emphasis: The aortic valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure at the end of isovolumetric contraction

rationales.a: Isovolumetric relaxation begins after ejection, when the aortic valve closes.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q015.takeaway: As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately more than systole, limiting ventricular filling time.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q015.displayText:
As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately more than systole, limiting ventricular filling time.

The effect of increased heart rate on cardiac cycle is that it decreases the duration of diastole more
than systole.

‘The duration of systole is much more fixed than that of diastole, so when the heart rate is
increased, diastole is shortened to a much greater degree. Coronary blood flow and ventricular
filling occur in diastole.
emphasis: As heart rate rises, diastole shortens disproportionately more than systole, limiting ventricular filling time

rationales.a: Systole changes relatively little; both phases do not shorten equally.
rationales.b: The total cardiac cycle becomes shorter, not longer.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q016.takeaway: Electromechanical systole spans ventricular electrical activation from QRS onset through mechanical systole to the second heart sound.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH28_Q016.displayText:
Electromechanical systole spans ventricular electrical activation from QRS onset through mechanical systole to the second heart sound.

510 

Electromechanical systole is the time interval between Q wave and second heart sound.

To record this both ECG and phonocardiography are required.

Electromechanical systole
emphasis: Electromechanical systole spans ventricular electrical activation from QRS onset through mechanical systole to the second heart sound

rationales.a: Q wave to T wave is the electrical QT interval and omits mechanical systolic time after repolarization.
rationales.b: S wave to T wave begins after ventricular depolarization and excludes electromechanical activation.
rationales.c: R wave to S1 misses the full mechanical ejection interval and the second sound endpoint.
